newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Beating death pinned on S.Korean student radicals.
newsitem.headline: Beating death pinned on S.Korean student radicals.

text.p: A South Korean pro-Pyongyang student group on Wednesday took responsibility for the death of a man it admitted beating during an interrogation as a suspected police informer.
A leader of the outlawed Hanchongryon group told a news conference at Hanyang University the victim died in his sleep after being beaten and bound on the campus during the night.
"We are ready to take full responsibility," said Lee Jun-koo, dressed in a black suit and black tie. His group is branded by the South Korean government as an agent of rival North Korea.
"We are ready to cooperate with police so long as a fair investigation is promised," the leader said.
Prime Minister Koh Kun called for speedy arrests, and ordered an emergency meeting of security-related ministers on Thursday, an official at his office said.
"The Prime Minister has ordered a quick arrest of those connected to the death at Hanyang University," the official said.
Earlier, a police official identified the victim as Lee Suk, 22, an office worker from Suwon. The official denied the man was a police informer.
The Hanchongryon leader said the victim had tried to strangle a student interrogating him in a room. Other students burst in, bound the man's wrists and battered him.

During his interrogation, the man signed a written confession that he was an informer, the student leader said. The man spent the night in a room with two students, who found him lifeless in the morning.
The police official said the corpse was covered in bruises when it was delivered to Hanyang University's teaching hospital by two students, who immediately fled.

Hanyang has been at the centre of six days of frequently violent protests in Seoul to demand the resignation of President Kim Young-sam. Hundreds of radical students are now holed up on the leafy campus grounds.

A police officer died on Monday during clashes around the campus with students wielding iron pipes and firebombs. But an autopsy on Tuesday found he probably died after being it by a police vehicle, not at the hands of students.
The Hanchongryon has been trying to stage a ceremony at Hanyang to inaugurate new office holders.
The student leader called on police to allow radical students on the campus to return home, while promising to indefinitely postpone the inauguration ceremonies.
"We ask that police not crack down on Hanchongryon over this incident," he said. Students were ready to fight if police tried to raid the campus.

But as night fell, police reinforcements poured in to streets around the campus, which was already ringed by helmeted riot officers in fireproof suits. Police checked the identities of all students entering and leaving.
Last August, police backed by helicopters staged a military-style assault at dawn on another Seoul campus to end violent protests led by the Hanchongryon.
Subsequently, 151 Hanchongryon leaders were arrested in a crackdown that appeared to cripple its organisation. Authorities say the organisation takes its orders from Pyongyang.

But the group is now riding a wave of public anger against President Kim in the wake of a bribery scandal involving Kim's son, and allegations that Kim grossly overspent during 1992 presidential elections.
Since the latest round of student unrest began last Friday, 215 police officers have been injured, 40 severely, according to police figures.
One student is recovering from brain surgery after being injured in hand-to-hand combat outside Hanyang on Monday.
